Tiny Hot Hatch Just Sold for Porsche Money, Has a Punchy V6 Behind the Seats and a Fatty Widebody
25 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
This car is not the usual hatchback that gets you from point A to point B with zero excitement. It is, in fact, quite the opposite. The TWR-modified Renault Clio will get you from point A to point B, but you'll want to take the longcut on your way to your destination. It has a V6 behind the front seats, over 200 horsepower, and thrilling road manners.
This 2001 Renault Clio was just sold for $90,000. Scrap everything you know about the standard French hatchback. All those are no longer valid. This car comes with a mid-mounted 3.0-liter V6 petrol engine, which produces 230 horsepower. Not exactly your usual Clio, right?
A manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels, which translates to fun behind the wheel, because what you are looking at is one of the most radical factory engineering experiments in automotive history.
Renault took a humble, front-wheel-drive economy commuter tiny car and converted it into the wide-body, mid-engine, rear-wheel-drive monster that you are looking at right now, rubbing your eyes in wonder, unable to understand how someone would pay luxury car money for a tiny hot hatch .
Photo: Cars and Bids The Clio V6 was designed as a sort of spiritual successor to the 1980s Renault 5 Turbo rally legend . Renault unveiled the concept car that previewed it at the 1998 Paris Motor Show as a promotional platform for the Clio V6 Trophy single-make racing series.
But the public went completely wild for it, so the French automaker decided to build a road-going variant. Because Renault's own production lines in Dieppe were busy, they partnered up with Tom Walkinshaw Racing (TWR). The Phase 1 cars were engineered by TWR, had their bodies modified in Finland, and were hand-assembled at TWR’s facility in Uddevalla, Sweden.
To transform a city hatchback into a mid-engine supercar slayer, TWR essentially threw out everything from the front seats backward. The tiny Renault no longer needed anything else. Where the rear bench seat used to be, a structural steel bulkhead was welded.
The 3.0-liter 24-valve V6 engine with naturally aspirated firepower was stuffed sideways into that space. The V6 wasn’t much of an exotic build. It was a modified version of the ES9 V6 used in family haulers such as the Renault Laguna or the Espace minivans.
Photo: Cars and Bids TWR upgraded the power unit with higher-compression pistons, lighter flywheels, and reworked induction ports to bump output to 230 horsepower (233 metric horsepower) and 221 pound-feet (300 Newton meters) of torque.
The engine puts the power down through the rear wheels with the help of the purists’ favorite, a six-speed manual transmission, hooked up to a limited-slip differential. Because the V6 engine had to be mounted transversely, right behind the cockpit where the rear seats used to be, space was incredibly tight.
Renault and Tom Walkinshaw Racing couldn't use a traditional rear-wheel-drive longitudinal gearbox. To achieve a manual transaxle compact enough to sit sideways but strong enough to withstand that amount of torque, Renault adapted the PK6 casing. TWR re-engineered the internals, the linkage setup, and the gear ratios to suit a high-revving sports car.
The new setup did not leave much room for a luggage compartment. The entire trunk was gone. Instead, owners got a tiny 45-liter cargo net behind the front seats and a small 7-liter plastic bucket under the front hood.
Photo: Cars and Bids Because the radiator also sat under the same hood, that space was basically a rolling oven, which meant you could not put groceries there. They would have been cooked by the time you got home.
The car comes with a body kit that makes it absurdly wide, which makes it intimidating next to the stock Clio. It features massive flared wheel arches, gaping side intakes to feed and cool the mid-mounted engine, and rides on 17-inch OZ racing wheels.
Surprisingly, while the exterior looked like that of a track-ready car, the interior was largely standard, sporting the then-cheap Clio layout, in which bucket seats upholstered in Alcantara were installed. A number plaque on the center console confirmed that the car was actually something special.
How special? 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.0 seconds special. A top speed of 146 mph (235 kph) special. With the very short wheelbase, a lightweight construction, and a rigid suspension out back, the driver has to know his way around the rear-wheel-drive pocket rocket to prevent uncontrollable tail dancing .
Photo: Cars and Bids Only 1,513 such cars saw the light of day between 2001 and 2003, and the one that just sold for $90,000 is one of them. Because these cars were never legally imported brand-new in the United States, they are the highly coveted forbidden fruit for American collectors.
However, now that early 2001 models cross the 25-year threshold required for legal U.S. import, pristine, low-mileage survivors like this 30,281-kilometer (18,815-mile) example have skyrocketed into genuine collector status.
Finished in Iceberg Silver with a blue and gray interior, the Renault-badged missile has just been handed over to its new owner with one key, Japanese-language service records, and a couple of flaws like scratches on the front plastic lip spoiler and bumper, along with signs of wear on the center console trim and shifter boot.
However, those flaws did not scare the buyer off. he paid Porsche Cayenne money for a tiny Renault that won’t win him races at the track, but will surely shock other motorists when flashing from stoplight to stoplight.
